topic: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
parentTitle: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
title: The therapeutic relationship and boundaries
blurb: Build and end a therapeutic relationship using Peplau's phases, keep clear boundaries, and listen well to people in distress or psychosis.
question: Liam, 30, has been on an acute ward for 6 weeks. He tells his named nurse she is 'the only one who understands him', asks for her personal phone number for after discharge and offers her a watch as thanks. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: In mental health nursing the relationship between nurse and person is itself a therapeutic tool. Hildegard Peplau's interpersonal relations model (1952) describes it as a purposeful, time-limited partnership that helps the person grow. It differs from friendship: it exists for the person's benefit, has an agreed purpose and an end, and the nurse holds the responsibility for keeping it safe. Plain English: warm and genuine, but always professional and always about them.

items.label: Meet, build trust, agree purpose and limits
Person identifies problems and who can help
Person makes full use of help on offer
Goals met; relationship ends and independence grows

teach.caption: 'Exploitation' here means making use of services, not taking advantage. Plan the ending from the start.

rows.label: Self-disclosure
values: Limited, only if it helps them

head: Clause
What it requires
rows: Clear professional boundaries with current and former patients and families
Refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality
Never ask for or accept loans from people in your care
Share information only when safety overrides confidentiality
teach.caption: NMC social media guidance: do not use social networks to build or pursue relationships with patients.

teach.h: Warning signs of a boundary slipping
teach.caption: Talk to your supervisor early: boundaries are a team responsibility.

items: Give time and privacy; sit at an angle, open posture, calm voice.
Use open questions and reflect back feelings: 'It sounds frightening.'
Summarise to check understanding; tolerate silence.
Acknowledge feelings and avoid arguing (NG10 de-escalation principles).

teach.body: When a person describes a delusion or hallucination, arguing that it is not real tends to escalate distress and damage trust, while agreeing with it (colluding) reinforces it. Instead, acknowledge the experience and the feeling it causes ('I can't hear the voices, but I can see they are upsetting you'), stay honest, focus on safety and the here and now, and keep sentences short and clear.
teach.cite: NICE NG10 de-escalation principles; good practice

teach.body: Liam's words and requests are signs the relationship is drifting from therapeutic to personal. The nurse thanks him warmly but declines the watch (Code 21.1) and does not give her personal number (20.6). She explains kindly that their work together ends at discharge and talks about who will support him next, linking him with his care coordinator. She records the conversation and discusses it in supervision so the team can plan a well-supported ending.

teach.text: Boundaries are the NURSE's responsibility, not the patient's, and the Code applies to FORMER patients too. Also, 'exploitation' in Peplau's model is a positive phase: the person making full use of the help available.

items: Peplau: orientation, identification, exploitation, resolution; plan the ending from the start.
Code 20.6 boundaries with current and former patients; 21.1 refuse all but trivial gifts; 21.2 no loans.
No social media contact to build relationships with patients.
Active listening: open questions, reflection, summarising; with psychosis, acknowledge feelings without arguing or colluding.

summary: You can now describe Peplau's phases and use them to start, work through and end a therapeutic relationship. You can also apply the Code to boundaries, gifts and social media, and listen effectively to people who are distressed or psychotic.

A.q: In Peplau's model, during which phase does the nurse first establish trust and agree the purpose of working together?
options: Identification
Exploitation
Resolution
Orientation
A.why: Orientation is the first phase: nurse and person meet, build trust and agree purpose and limits.

whyNot.0: Identification follows, when the person identifies problems and helpers.
whyNot.1: Exploitation is when the person makes full use of the help offered.
whyNot.2: Resolution is the ending of the relationship.

A.q: A patient's family offers a nurse an expensive bottle of perfume at discharge. Which NMC Code requirement applies?
options: Accept it if it is declared to the manager
Refuse all but the most trivial gifts
Accept it if the patient has now been discharged
Share it with the team to avoid favouritism
A.why: Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality that might be interpreted as an attempt to gain preferential treatment.

whyNot.0: Declaring an expensive gift does not make accepting it consistent with 21.1.
whyNot.2: Discharge does not change the gift rule.
whyNot.3: Sharing a non-trivial gift is still accepting it.

A.q: A former patient sends a nurse a friend request on social media 3 months after discharge. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Decline it, as boundaries apply to former patients
Accept it, as the person is no longer in her care now
Accept it but restrict what he can see
Accept it if he is well and back at work
A.why: Code 20.6 requires clear professional boundaries with current and former patients; NMC social media guidance warns against using social networks to build relationships with patients.

whyNot.2: Restricting the view still creates a personal relationship online.
whyNot.3: His recovery does not remove the professional boundary.

B.q: Mr Ahmed, who has psychosis, says angrily, 'The television is sending messages about me.' Which response is most therapeutic?
options: 'That's impossible; televisions can't do that.'
'Which channel is it? I'll watch it with you.'
'That sounds really unsettling. How are you feeling?'
'Let's not talk about that; it's just your illness.'
B.why: Acknowledging the feeling without arguing or agreeing keeps trust and reduces distress, in line with de-escalation principles (acknowledge feelings, avoid arguing).

whyNot.0: Arguing about the belief tends to escalate distress.
whyNot.1: Offering to watch with him colludes with the delusion.
whyNot.3: Dismissing it closes the conversation and invalidates his distress.

B.q: A newly qualified nurse tells a patient about her own divorce in detail 'to build rapport'. What is the main concern?
options: It breaches confidentiality about her former partner
Self-disclosure should serve the patient, not the nurse
Nurses must not share any personal information
It should be recorded as a clinical intervention
B.why: In a therapeutic relationship, any self-disclosure should be limited and used purposefully for the person's benefit; detailed personal sharing shifts the focus to the nurse and blurs boundaries.

whyNot.0: It is mainly her own story; the core problem is whose needs the disclosure serves.
whyNot.2: Brief, purposeful self-disclosure can sometimes help; detail for the nurse's needs does not.
whyNot.3: Recording does not fix an inappropriate disclosure.

B.q: Which nurse response is an example of reflection in active listening?
options: 'Why did you stop taking your tablets?'
'You must feel better now you're here.'
'Let me tell you what helped another patient.'
'You sound let down by the people around you.'
B.why: Reflection mirrors back the feeling the nurse has heard, showing understanding and inviting the person to say more.

whyNot.0: 'Why' questions can sound judgemental and are not reflection.
whyNot.1: This tells the person how they feel rather than reflecting it.
whyNot.2: This shifts focus away from the person's experience.

C.q: Liam's discharge is in 2 weeks. He becomes low and says, 'There's no point. You're leaving me like everyone else.' Using Peplau's model, what is the best approach?
options: Delay his discharge until he no longer feels this way
Promise to stay in touch by phone after discharge
Acknowledge the loss and work through the planned ending
Hand his care to another nurse straight away
C.why: Resolution involves ending the relationship in a planned way, acknowledging feelings about loss, reviewing progress and linking to ongoing support, while assessing his low mood and risk.

whyNot.0: Endings are part of the relationship; delaying discharge avoids, not resolves, the issue.
whyNot.1: Personal contact after discharge breaches boundaries.
whyNot.3: An abrupt switch would confirm his fear of abandonment.

C.q: A healthcare assistant tells you that a colleague has been meeting a recently discharged patient for coffee and lending her money. What should you do?
options: Raise the concern with your manager without delay
Speak to the colleague and keep it between you
Ask the patient whether she minds the contact
Wait to see whether the patient complains
C.why: This suggests breaches of Code 20.6 (boundaries with former patients) and 21.2 (loans) and possible exploitation of a vulnerable person; raise the concern promptly through the organisation's process.

whyNot.1: Keeping it private leaves the patient unprotected.
whyNot.2: The responsibility lies with professionals, not the patient.
whyNot.3: Waiting leaves a possible safeguarding risk unaddressed.

C.q: During your first meeting with Ms Chen, newly admitted with severe anxiety, which action best fits the orientation phase?
options: Set her long-term recovery goals with her today
Explain your role, how often you'll meet and the ending
Encourage her to join every ward group from tomorrow
Review with her what she has achieved since admission
C.why: Orientation involves introductions, explaining the nurse's role, agreeing purpose, frequency and the expected ending, and starting to build trust.

whyNot.0: Detailed goals come later, once problems are identified.
whyNot.2: Making full use of services is the exploitation phase.

reteach.title: Purposeful, time-limited, for them
reteach.question: What makes a relationship therapeutic rather than social?

blocks.body: Ask: Whose needs does this meet? (the person's). Is there an agreed purpose? (recovery goals). Is there a planned ending? (yes, from the start). If the answer to the first is 'mine', a boundary is slipping: talk to your supervisor.

blocks.text: Boundaries apply to former patients too (Code 20.6).

explain.body: Orientation (trust, purpose), identification (problems, helpers), exploitation (using help fully), resolution (ending, independence).

test.q: In Peplau's model, what does the 'exploitation' phase mean?
options: The nurse takes advantage of the person's trust
The person makes full use of the help available
The relationship is ended and reviewed
The person first meets the nurse
test.why: Exploitation is a positive phase in which the person makes full use of the services and help offered.

whyNot.0: The term does not carry its everyday negative meaning here.

explain.body: 20.6 clear boundaries with current and former patients and families; 21.1 refuse all but trivial gifts; 21.2 no loans; responsible social media use.

test.q: A patient's relative offers to lend a nurse money to help with her car repairs. Which Code clause is most relevant?
options: 21.2: do not ask for or accept loans
10.3: do not falsify records
14.2: explain and apologise after harm
18.4: store medicines securely
test.why: Code 21.2: never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them.

whyNot.2: 14.2 is the duty to explain and apologise after an error or harm, not a rule on loans.

explain.body: Open questions, reflecting feelings, summarising, tolerating silence, open posture and calm voice.

test.q: Which is an open question suitable for starting a conversation with a distressed patient?
options: 'Are you feeling suicidal today?'
'Did you sleep last night?'
'What has today been like for you?'
'Is it your mum who upset you?'
test.why: Open questions invite the person to talk in their own words; the others can be answered yes or no.

whyNot.0: This is closed; direct questions about suicide are vital but come within the assessment.

explain.body: Do not argue or collude. Acknowledge the experience and feeling, stay honest, focus on safety and the present, use short clear sentences.

test.q: A patient says, 'The voices are telling me the staff will poison me.' What is the best first response?
options: 'The voices are lying; nobody wants to hurt you.'
'Then don't eat the food today.'
'Try to tune out the voices and watch the TV instead.'
'That must be frightening. Tell me more about it.'
test.why: Acknowledging the fear without arguing or colluding builds trust and allows the nurse to assess risk, such as refusing food or acting on the voices.

whyNot.0: Arguing with the content can increase distress and mistrust.
whyNot.1: This colludes with the belief and risks harm.
whyNot.2: Distraction before acknowledging his fear dismisses the experience and misses the risk.
